scopes.prerequisites: Public-source access only. No local profile, GPU or liveness result is required for this durable algorithm/scheduling comparison.

Finite question: For non-LLM GPU sparse triangular solve (SpTRSV) used in sparse direct/iterative solvers, compare dependency-level scheduling with one or two dependency-driven ready-queue / atomic-counter or hybrid row schedules. How do dependency depth, level width, row-length skew, multiple right-hand sides, preprocessing/reuse count, queue/atomic contention, temporary metadata, synchronization and numerical ordering determine when each design wins or loses? Keep the shared sparse representation fixed when comparing schedulers so this is not a storage-format survey. Focus on the DAG-specific work assignment and readiness protocol, including how a ready row becomes visible safely to consumers; do not assume one implementation detail is portable between backends.

Evidence requirements: Use at least two independently implemented GPU libraries or original research implementations, with official API/source documentation and original papers or maintainer technical reports. Suitable source families include cuSPARSE SpSV, rocSPARSE sparse triangular solve, Ginkgo/Kokkos/oneMKL implementations, and papers authored by the implementing groups; select sources with exact URLs, releases/revisions, hardware and license/provenance. Use no more than seven substantive primary URLs. Compare at least three concrete scheduling strategies in one table: level-scheduled rows with level barriers, dependency-counter/ready-frontier scheduling, and a hybrid (for example, level batches with intra-level row balancing or dependency queues with bounded local aggregation). Cover narrow/deep versus broad/shallow dependency graphs and uniform versus skewed row work; include measured published wins and at least one counterexample where queueing/metadata or level synchronization favors the simpler method. Where sources do not provide comparable workloads, say so instead of manufacturing a direct ranking. Distinguish measured data from your analysis and state transfer limits.

Give a compact cost model for preprocessing and per-solve work over repeated solves, live metadata/temporary storage, atomic updates and barriers, with explicit assumptions; include a single future experiment design that would discriminate the methods on a representative scientific matrix without running it. Keep any suggested hardware metrics to those that measure the specific distinction.

Novelty guard: R759 covers broad persistent-worker/scan/work partition methods; R763 broadly surveys non-LLM pipeline/residency, data reuse and irregular tasks; R778 compares sparse storage formats for SpMV/SpMM; R779 covers irregular resident gathers, coalescing and address-translation mechanisms; R786 studies graph aggregation fan-in and floating-point reduction; R813 concerns grouped MoE/expert work. R839 is bank mapping and local-memory layout, not DAG scheduling. This report must center on sparse triangular dependency readiness and scheduling, not generic worklists, graph frontier traversal/aggregation, sparse format conversion, global memory transaction/TLB behavior, generic scans, or GPU pipeline fusion. Do not propose a Strata code change or claim Arc/B570 performance.

Finite question: For non-LLM 2-D CNN convolution on GPUs and, where primary evidence allows, systolic/ASIC accelerators, compare three ways to map convolution onto compute: explicit im2col materialization followed by GEMM, implicit-GEMM indexing without materializing the lowered matrix, and direct spatial/output tiling that reuses input windows. Center the comparison on when extra materialization and workspace are repaid by regular matrix execution, versus when address generation, input reuse, boundary waste, channel/tile underfill or local-storage pressure change the result. Use 3x3 stride-1 as the primary family and 1x1 or strided convolution as a contrasting regime; include Winograd only if the report can keep it bounded to small-filter tradeoffs and its numerical/transform-cost evidence. Analyze at least two exact shapes/batches and preserve each source's dtype, padding/layout and measurement boundary.

Evidence requirements: Use official API/developer docs and original implementation sources (for example, cuDNN algorithm documentation, CUTLASS implicit-GEMM convolution docs/source, oneDNN implementation docs/source) together with original convolution mapping/accelerator papers or original maintainer technical reports. Use at most seven substantive primary URLs and pin source release/revision, accelerator, software version, shape and metric for every performance claim. Compare at least three concrete algorithms in one table including temporary bytes and extra passes, launch/host setup where available, input/weight/output reuse, arithmetic/workspace, boundary handling and known applicability. Include at least one measured case where each of two different mapping families wins and a counterexample where its overhead, workspace, transform or shape regime makes it lose; if a source does not support such comparisons, state the gap and avoid false like-for-like conclusions. Distinguish algorithm analysis from measured results. Do not present published performance as a Strata/Intel Arc prediction.

Give a compact break-even model that accounts for lowered-tensor materialization bytes and passes, direct-index address work, matrix-engine utilization, spatial reuse and temporary-storage peak. Explain numerical risks where algorithm transforms change rounding. Provide one future experiment design only, with a controlled shape set and metrics sufficient to separate materialization cost from kernel compute; do not execute it.

Novelty guard: R798 covers skinny/ragged and dense GEMM output-tile geometry; R805 covers Intel matrix operand layout lowering; R811 covers 2-D block-message descriptors and alignment; R813 covers grouped MoE execution; R832 covers in-kernel producer/consumer pipeline roles; R835 covers stencil temporal blocking/halo costs; R839 covers local-memory bank layout. This report must study convolution algorithm mapping, implicit versus explicit lowering, spatial input reuse and workspace—not another GEMM tile/operand-layout survey, generic operator fusion report, stencil time-step reuse survey, barrier/prefetch design, or Strata adoption proposal.
